method: Each finding was reviewed against the pull request's full diff on GitHub, not only the lines the finding cites.

verdicts.note: Docstring only: a warning block was added to edit. No code change.
Comment only: renames MaybeStripAnsi to _PagerWriter in a comment. The hasattr check still holds.
Swaps new EmptyObject() for Object.create(null). Both have no Object methods; only prototype identity changes.
Annotation widened to _PDataSerializer[t.Any]. The tool correctly said no caller is affected, so it should not be a finding.
filename type widened to accept os.PathLike. The caller passes text; the tool's "not affected" is right.
Type level only. The Protocol dumps lost **kwargs, but the runtime serializer is json, which takes skipkeys, and tests are not type checked.
Command.main's except chain was rewritten, but exit codes, the "Aborted!" message, and non-standalone propagation are preserved.
Label wrong: the return value did change (a set became an ordered list), but UsageError.show uses max(key=len), so only equal-length ties differ.
The returned expression changed textually but not in value: get_help_spec returns make_metavar, and spec has the old human_readable_name body.

Label wrong ("internally only"). parseQuery's result went from {} to a null-prototype object, so hasOwnProperty, toString and other Object methods disappear, and $URL.query and getQuery hand it straight to users.
Receiver misresolved. serializer is a Serializer, whose dumps(obj, salt=None) still takes salt; the tool matched the Protocol's dumps by name.
Typing only: Path was made generic over path_type. Runtime behaviour is unchanged.

underRated.note: A real behaviour change reported as low severity and labelled "internally only": parseQuery's result changed from a plain object to a null-prototype object.

failurePatterns.pattern: Findings are emitted even when the tool itself concludes that no caller is affected.
Comment and docstring edits count as changes.
Return-value changes are missed by the "internals only" label, because only return expressions are compared, not how the returned value is built.
Name-based method resolution picks the wrong class.
Protocol signatures are treated as runtime contracts.
